extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and educated readers interested in the logic of science and probability (naturalists, statisticians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the conception and calculation of probability and the logical use of continuity and relative numbers in scientific reasoning, with concrete rules (Direct, Addition, Multiplication) and philosophical caveats about single cases and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of continuity in forming conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of continuous quantity is a powerful aid to the formation of true and fruitful conceptions; it breaks greatest differences down into differences of degree and aids generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalists use the idea of continuity to find intermediate forms and build general conceptions (example: S-shaped vs C-shaped markings). Caution: excessive use of number can narrow thought and produce pettiness; continuity may be introduced even where it does not strictly exist, as a useful fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as quantitative logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of probabilities is simply the science of logic quantitatively treated: 1 and 0 mark certainties of truth/falsity; intermediate fractions mark degrees to which evidence leans toward truth or falsity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general problem is to determine, from given facts, the numerical probability of a possible fact — i.e., how much the given facts are worth as evidence. This framing supports the application of arithmetic to logical inference but invites careful examination of limits and disputes in foundational principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability defined as proportion of successful inferences (frequency conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the probability of a mode of argument as the proportion of cases in which that mode carries truth with it (the ratio of times both premise A and conclusion B are true to the total times A is true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception relies on repeated inferences: ratios show fluctuations early but approach a fixed limit over thousands/millions of cases. It grounds rules for calculating probabilities but implies that single isolated inferences are either true or false (no middle term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Always state the conditioning (probabilities are conditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of the probability of the event B without naming the condition (the antecedent A) really has no meaning at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid elliptical language that omits the condition; such vagueness fosters a mistaken view of causation and 'inherent chance'. When the condition is obvious it may be omitted, but contracting the habit leads to vague thinking and persistent errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-case limitations of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability properly belongs to modes of inference repeated indefinitely; an individual inference is either true or false and, by itself, admits no probabilistic intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, for practical decision-making (e.g., choosing between two risky packs with different proportions), it is reasonable to prefer the option with higher probability even for a unique, high-stakes case. Philosophically this tension motivates extending concern to an indefinite community or long-run perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicality presupposes social/unlimited interests
rubrics_metrics.description: To be fully logical in collective inferences, one must identify one's interests with an indefinite community extending beyond personal fate; logicality is rooted in the social principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to justify reasoning that prioritizes long-run/probabilistic success over isolated cases. Practical implication: adopt standards of judgment that would be accepted by someone whose interests embrace the whole (possibly unlimited) community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule I — Direct calculation of relative numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate directly any relative number (e.g., average passengers per trip): count the number for each unit (trip), add them, and divide by the number of units (trips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplifications apply when each individual relate belongs exclusively to one correlate (example: inhabitants per dwelling — divide total inhabitants by dwellings). Caveat: this direct division fails when individuals can belong to multiple correlates (example: passengers making multiple trips). For probabilities: compute proportion of cases where A and B both occur divided by total cases where A occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule II — Addition of relative numbers (mutually exclusive classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two relative numbers with the same correlate (e.g., x's per y and z's per y), the number of x's and z's together per y is the sum of the two given numbers, provided nothing belongs at once to both classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average number of friends plus average number of enemies equals average number of persons interested in a man. Anti-pattern: do not add overlapping classes (e.g., different exemption causes for military service) without accounting for shared membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule III — Multiplication of relative numbers (nested relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The product of two relative numbers (x's per y times z's per x of y) gives the relative number of z's per y (example: average teeth per child times children per family = average children's teeth per family), subject to restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions: fails if a relate can belong to multiple correlates or if correlates share items (e.g., same child in multiple families). Applied to probabilities: multiply P(B|A) by P(C|B) to get P(C|A) when classes are chosen so conditional probabilities are consistent and independence assumptions hold approximately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary rule (assumed equality of conditional probabilities / pragmatic independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the probability that C is true if B is is substantially the same as the probability that C is true if A; when so, one may multiply probabilities in a simplified way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is convenient but not universally valid — exercise double caution: (1) do not use it where it will cause serious error, and (2) do use it when legitimately applicable. Example: proportion of male births overall approximates that in any season in New York, allowing multiplication to get joint probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check independence carefully; do not assume it blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether two events may be treated as independent is often a subtle empirical question; assuming independence without verification can produce significant errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in card games, insufficient shuffling creates dependence (observable deviation from theoretical counts, e.g., counting spades over many hands showed 94 vs expected 85 hands with 3–4 spades). In life-applications independence is often harder to justify than in idealized urn problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of fictions/idealizations in scientific reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the idea of continuity or other idealizations where they do not strictly exist can be useful in science (fictions sometimes have great utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include using continuous distributions (Quetelet, Galton) to study biological and social matters. Recognize these are pragmatic tools that aid generalization though they may not reflect literal facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about errors and unsettled foundations in probability literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Many treatises on probability contain indefensible solutions; the subject involves subtleties and disputes over fundamental principles, and lacks a single regular method of procedure in some extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: make the idea of probability perfectly clear before extending probabilistic calculus to more recondite questions; rely on careful analysis rather than unquestioned formulae.
